articles.title: Lavender's first job: make Mossdeep punt
articles.dek: The Eclipse have plenty of spectacular numbers. Mara Voss starts with the possession that ended at 0:37 and the touchdown that followed eight seconds later.
articles.author: mara-voss

body.text: I want Lavender to make Mossdeep punt before anyone starts telling me what this matchup means for the Indigo Bowl. One punt. A normal, recognizable change of possession in which Dram Marino has to leave the field because the defense finished its assignment. Lavaridge never managed it. Until an opponent can produce that ordinary inconvenience, the grander discussion is mostly giving the Eclipse something pleasant to read.

Mossdeep scored 41 points, gained 456 yards and handed Ninjaskamara four touchdowns' worth of work. Those are easy numbers to admire. The number I keep returning to is zero in the punt column. Michael Dorrill's offense had incomplete passes, settled for two field goals and did not convert every third down. It still never handed the Inferno a routine punt possession. That's an enormous amount of control over the afternoon.

I wrote last week that I enjoyed the other 46 points in the 49–3 win over Fuchsia, too. Fine. I still do. This week I want to discuss why the points kept arriving without the assistance of a return touchdown. The answer is in a combination that should worry Travis Scarboro: the Eclipse can win a short-yardage exchange on defense and immediately refuse to play short-yardage football on offense.

With 37 seconds left in the first half, Lavaridge faced fourth-and-two. Delphox was sacked. The play names DurrickBurgess, now a Conkeldurr; the individual box score splits the sack between him and Shawn Mareman. Either way, the possession ended. Eight seconds later Marino threw deep left to Ninjaskamara for a forty-yard touchdown. A defense made one decisive stop, and its offense treated the next snap as a chance to take the whole field.

That is the sequence I would put first in Lavender's preparation. There is no reason to invent an offensive formation or a coverage mistake the record doesn't identify. The documented choice is enough: first-and-ten, deep left, forty yards, touchdown. Mossdeep did not use the late possession merely to collect a few harmless yards and consider a kick. It had a halfback who could finish a deep pass.
I don't want the clock to make me careless. But if the throw is there, passing it up is a decision, too. He gave us a chance to finish the half with seven. The protection let me take it.
body.speaker: Dram Marino

body.text: Stop calling the whole thing a running game

Ninjaskamara ran for one hundred yards and caught passes for 113. Calling him a rushing threat captures less than half his yardage in this game. The forty-yard touchdown wasn't even his longest reception; he also had a 48-yard catch. Lavender's problem is a player who can turn a handoff into a score up the middle, take a run right for another, and then make the defense defend a deep pass to the left.

That does not mean the rest of the offense can be ignored. Marshall Flock had twelve carries, the same as Ninjaskamara, and gained 77 yards. Gronkaludon caught four for 57. Seven Mossdeep players caught passes. The Eclipse can ask several different players to make the manageable gain while waiting for their best finisher to make a very large one. That's why chasing the headline player around the field is an incomplete plan.

The protection is the other part I would refuse to discuss vaguely. Marino was not sacked. Gene Shuckshaw and Shuck Bednarik each recorded a 100 percent block-win figure, and Bastony Boseli collected twelve pancakes. Those are broad game totals, not proof of who blocked whom on the forty-yard score. They still tell Lavender that creating pressure will require something more persuasive than hoping a talented front eventually gets through.

At the other end, Derrat Brooks made ten tackles and four tackles for loss. Lavaridge ran eleven times for fifteen yards and failed on all seven third-down attempts. I get impatient when a blowout becomes a conversation exclusively about offensive glamour. Mossdeep's defense repeatedly created situations where the Inferno had to find the answer through Delphox, then ended enough of those possessions to keep the entire game moving in one direction.
A fair test for a rested opponent

Lavender brings a 4–1 record and a bye into this game. It also brings a season scoring margin of plus-one. I am not dismissing the four wins; the Wails earned them. I am asking what kind of contest they have to build to earn a fifth. A wide-open exchange against a team with 244 points in six games seems an unnecessarily generous invitation. The first target should be fewer Mossdeep possessions that end in points.

My checkable standard is three Eclipse punts and no Mossdeep completion of thirty yards or more. That is a demanding combination, and it is meant to be. If Lavender can repeatedly end possessions and remove the giant pass from the scorebook, its own offense gets a game it can manage. If it cannot, a close fourth-quarter script may never become available. Rest helps a team prepare; it doesn't award any first downs.

For Mossdeep, I want the same discipline that made this win so severe: no giveaways and protection that holds up when the opponent knows what is coming. The Eclipse's two most recent wins total ninety points scored and six allowed. There is no need to manufacture an argument that those games were secretly difficult. There is a need to recognize that Lavender will arrive with a different opportunity and a full week to study the methods.

I would begin that study with the fourth-and-two at 0:37. Then I would play the next snap. I would let the room see Ninjaskamara finish the forty yards, and I would ask the defense how it plans to prevent the next version. The answer has to be better than hoping Mossdeep finally feels like punting.

art.alt: Ninjaskamara, Ninjask No. 27, carrying a football in Mossdeep magenta and gold.

articles.title: Let Crem be Crem
articles.dek: Mt. Silver's replacement quarterback does not owe anyone an imitation. Ellis Quill on the useful, modest things that made a difficult afternoon survivable.
articles.author: ellis-quill

body.text: I don't think Crem Ftzpatrik owes Mt. Silver a convincing impression of Josh Alakazam. I think he owes it the next sensible throw. That sounds like an awfully small ambition for a 6–0 team, but an unbeaten record can make the people around a new quarterback ask for everything at once. Ftzpatrik did enough against Cianwood to deserve a week without being assigned somebody else's personality, arm or future.

Alakazam is out for the season, with sixteen weeks listed on the injury report. Garshawn Lynch remains out for five more. The Reds have spent consecutive victories losing players who helped make those victories seem likely. There is something particularly disorienting about winning while the season keeps changing shape. The standings tell you to celebrate. The next day's preparation tells you to begin again in several important places.

Ftzpatrik completed fifteen of eighteen passes for 135 yards, threw two touchdowns, and scored another on a one-yard run. He also threw an interception and took three sacks. I like that the complete line resists an instant fairy tale. A reserve came in and did useful work. Some of it was difficult. Some of it went wrong. The team won 27–7, and he can study the mistakes without having to carry a defeat along with them.
I don't really know what to say when people ask if this is my moment. Josh got hurt. I wanted to help. I'll be happier talking about a good throw than making it sound like I was waiting for that.
body.speaker: Crem Ftzpatrik

body.text: That seems a reasonable distinction to me. It also gives Connor McLarren a reasonable starting point. He can prepare the player he actually has, in the offense that is actually available, while recognizing how much the surrounding team contributed. The Reds allowed only seven points. Their runners gained 103 yards. Their receivers caught several modest passes that kept the offense from turning every new down into a new emergency.

Plusico Buress caught eight balls on eight targets. Tony Gyarzalez caught six on six. Together they supplied 104 receiving yards without a touchdown. I suspect those lines will be read quickly beneath the quarterback news. They deserve a longer pause. A replacement quarterback can be helped enormously by a receiver who finishes the available catch rather than requiring a perfect dramatic throw to contribute.
The useful apology is the next catch

Buress had been part of the trouble at Oreburgh the week before. His late fumble made that 24–20 escape more dangerous. Against Cianwood, the Reds did not lose a fumble. I am wary of calling every better afternoon redemption, as though a professional life is a collection of little courtroom scenes. Still, eight catches on eight chances is a fairly good way to answer an uncomfortable week.
I wanted him to throw with confidence. If that means eight ordinary catches, give me eight ordinary catches. I'll take them. Last week is there. It doesn't get to catch this week's football for me.
body.speaker: Plusico Buress

body.text: Ftzpatrik found Ariados for a fourteen-yard touchdown to the right in the second quarter and Raticate for eight to the same side in the fourth. Between them he scored on a one-yard run. I am not reading an entire offensive identity into three scoring plays. I am observing that the Reds found scores through several players and several kinds of work. They did not simply wait for a single replacement star to appear.

The interception belongs here, too. Golbat took the deep-left pass late in the first half. Beedrill and Victreebel supplied the sacks. The relief appearance was successful without being protected from unpleasant moments. That is more encouraging to me than a story in which every mistake is hidden behind the victory. A player who finishes the game after a bad throw has at least begun the work of handling the next one.

Mt. Silver's defense helped set the emotional temperature. Cianwood scored with 1:23 remaining, after the Reds had built a 27–0 lead. Before that, the Crushers lost a Bibarel fumble recovered by Stunky and a Gardevoir interception caught by Machamp. The defense gave the offense the sort of margin in which a cautious decision could remain merely cautious. Ftzpatrik was not asked to rescue a collapsing scoreboard on every possession.
Petalburg will ask something new

The next opponent is 5–1 Petalburg. The Pride just beat Mauville 21–9 and will have an opportunity to prepare for Ftzpatrik from the beginning. That changes the assignment. A relief quarterback enters a game already in motion; a likely starter becomes part of the other team's week's work. The Reds cannot know how that will go by looking only at a completion percentage from Cianwood.

They can know what helped. Raticate's ten carries for 66 yards helped. Vibrava's 27 yards helped. Buress and Gyarzalez finishing their catches helped. McLarren can build the next week's conversation around those contributions rather than beginning with a list of things Alakazam would have done. A missing starter leaves a large absence. Repeating the dimensions of that absence does not fill it.

I am not ready to move Mt. Silver out of the contender discussion. Six wins, a plus-109 margin and 45 points allowed are substantial accomplishments. I am also not ready to declare the quarterback problem solved because one afternoon ended well. Both reactions would make the story easier to tell than the season is likely to be. The Reds have earned a cushion; now they have to use it intelligently.

Ftzpatrik's first extended answer was modest enough to be believable: completed passes, two touchdown throws, a short scoring run, and a few errors the defense could withstand. I would let him keep that version of the afternoon. When Petalburg arrives, the first useful thing he can do is find an available receiver and put the ball where that receiver can catch it.

art.alt: Silver and red quarterback helmets numbered 7 and 12 beside a football.

articles.title: Eighteen carries. One hundred eight yards. Thank you.
articles.dek: Dorian Pike asked Cinnabar to pick up the ball. The Blaze answered with 27 points, a division win and a much more convincing running game.
articles.author: dorian-pike

body.text: Blaine, I would like to begin with a sincere expression of gratitude. Your football team carried the football eighteen times. It gained 108 yards. It scored two rushing touchdowns. It beat Pewter 27–10. These are beautiful, uncomplicated numbers, and I am prepared to admire them at considerable volume. Last week I asked Cinnabar to pick up the ball. This week Cinnabar picked it up and took it somewhere.

I know. The passing game had another productive afternoon. Gholdengo threw for 221 yards, Frogadier caught seven passes for 105, and Exploud caught seven for 69. I have eyes. I can enjoy those things while also noticing that a team with a useful quarterback became substantially harder to inconvenience when its rushing total stopped looking like a misplaced receiving line.

And here's the uncomfortable truth: the Blaze needed this response. Twelve carries for twenty-five yards in the previous loss at Dewford was a poor way to support a passing game capable of making an opponent defend the field. Eighteen for 108 against Pewter is six yards a carry. Six. You do not need a complicated speech to understand what six yards does for the next down.

Seismitoad led it with ten carries for 69 yards and a touchdown. Gholdengo added 22 on five and scored from two yards out. Pidgeotto supplied seventeen on three. Three different contributors, a sensible amount of work, and enough production to make a defender care about the handoff. I am not asking for a museum exhibit of old football. I am asking for an offense that presents more than one unpleasant choice.
I was happy they kept giving me chances. The blockers did a lot for me. If a run helps the next pass, that's good work, too. I don't need every useful carry to be the one that scores.
body.speaker: Seismitoad

body.text: Very gracious. Very considerate. Allow me to be less restrained on your behalf: 69 yards on ten carries is useful, and the 29-yard long gain is useful, and a five-yard touchdown up the middle early in the second quarter is useful. Cinnabar should make room for that usefulness again next week instead of treating it as a surprising guest who has to leave before dinner.
The part after thirteen to ten

The Blaze led 13–3 at halftime. Charjabug had made field goals from 51 and 24 yards, and Seismitoad had scored between them. Pewter then opened the third quarter with an eleven-yard touchdown pass from Wyrdeer to Yanmega. At 13–10, Cinnabar had reached the portion of a game where a favored team can begin behaving as if the lead itself ought to do the work.

The Blaze answered with actual work. Arcanine sacked Wyrdeer twice in the third quarter, once for eight yards and once for seven. Gholdengo scored on a two-yard run to the right with 1:45 left in the period. Octillery intercepted Wyrdeer forty-four seconds later and returned the ball nineteen yards. Cinnabar had a defense changing possessions and an offense finishing a chance on the ground.

That is how you keep a game from becoming a tribute to the opponent's resilience. You make the next useful play. Then you make another. A three-point lead became ten, and the fourth quarter brought a four-yard touchdown pass short right to Wigglytuff. One catch, one target, one touchdown. Wigglytuff contributed exactly the number of yards the situation required and declined to make the matter more complicated.

Gholdengo finished nineteen-for-31 with a touchdown, no interceptions and one sack taken. The quarterback did not need to throw every point onto the board. He could share the scoring with Seismitoad, contribute a short run himself and trust a defense that held Pewter to 199 total yards. The Blaze finished with 329. That is a substantial advantage in ordinary offensive production, and the final score reflected it.
Frogadier has been worth your attention

I also want the seven catches for 105 yards discussed properly. Frogadier caught seven of ten targets and had a long gain of 29. Those are receiving yards that repeatedly moved the offense, even though the touchdown pass went to somebody else. If you only count the names attached to scoring plays, you will miss much of the reason the Blaze were close enough to score them.
I liked being someone he could keep coming back to. The yards are nice. I would've liked to finish one in the end zone, but we got there through other guys. That was enough for this game.
body.speaker: Frogadier

body.text: Exploud's seven catches for 69 yards gave Gholdengo another reliable destination. Together those two receivers produced fourteen catches and 174 yards. The quarterback had room to move the ball through them, the runners had room to contribute, and the offense did not lose a fumble. This was a much fuller performance than a box score built around one large passing number and an apology for everything else.

The kicking was not perfect. Charjabug made two of three field goals, although all three extra points went through. There is the small piece of housekeeping I am willing to mention while enjoying a seventeen-point win. Oricorio also remains listed out for one week, so the secondary is still working around an absence. Neither fact requires pretending that the afternoon was less convincing than it was.

Cinnabar is 4–2 with 125 points scored, 71 allowed and a plus-54 margin. The Blaze lead the Kanto West in the current standings and hold the fourth conference playoff seed. Eterna comes next, carrying a 24–21 win at Snowpoint. That matchup gives Blaine another chance to demonstrate that the improved running game can remain part of the weekly offense, rather than an answer delivered once to shut up a columnist.
It did not shut up the columnist. Obviously.

I want Seismitoad involved again. I want the quarterback protected, Frogadier targeted and the defense finishing its pressure with the kind of sacks Arcanine supplied. The Blaze have just shown how all of those things can fit inside the same win. Eighteen carries. One hundred eight yards. Put those numbers where the next game plan can see them.

art.alt: Cinnabar orange and gold helmet beside a football on stadium turf.
